'''Zohra Aziza Baccouche''' (November 25, 1972{{Spaced en dash}}June 11, 2021) was an American physicist and science filmmaker. She was an [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Mass Media Science and Engineering fellow at [[CNN]] and founder and CEO of media company ''Aziza Productions''.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Obituary for Zohra Aziza Baccouche at Riddick Funeral Service |url=https://www.riddickfuneralservices.com/obituary/zohra-baccouche?lud=5EE311A883B8AC0D5F34A8D3E778B0ED |access-date=2022-04-27 |website=www.riddickfuneralservices.com |language=en}}</ref> Baccouche lost her sight due to a [[brain tumor]] at eight years old.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=CNN Transcript - Morning News: Aziza Baccouche Discusses Overcoming Blindness - August 11, 2000|url=http://edition.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0008/11/mn.20.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107010512/http://edition.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0008/11/mn.20.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 7, 2018|access-date=2018-11-06|website=CNN}}</ref> 

== Early life ==
Baccouche was born to an African-American mother and Tunisian father<ref name="Physics 2018">{{Cite web|last=Physics|first=Institute of|title=Once a physicist: Z Aziza Baccouche|url=http://www.iop.org/careers/working-life/articles/2017/page_69233.html|access-date=2018-11-06|website=www.iop.org|language=en-GB}}</ref> on November 25, 1972<ref name="POC2">{{Cite web|last=Squared|first=POC|title=Dr. Zohra Aziza Baccouche – Nuclear Physicist|date=25 January 2019 |url=https://poc2.co.uk/2019/01/25/dr-zohra-aziza-baccouche-nuclear-physicist|access-date=2020-06-10|language=en-GB}}</ref> and brought up in [[Tunisia]]. She developed a brain tumor as a child, which caused a disorder called [[hydrocephalus]] when she was eight years old. <ref name=":1" />  Hydrocephalus blocks cerebral fluid in the brain and creates pressure within the ventricles. In Baccouche's case, that pressure damaged her optic nerve causing her to lose all but 9% of her vision by the age of eight. <ref name=":0" />

== Education ==
Baccouche was the first blind person to study physics at the [[College of William & Mary]], graduating in 1995 with a [[Bachelor of Science]]. <ref name="Physics 2018" /> Her undergraduate advisor suggested that because she was blind, she should not study physics. <ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/spotlight-diversity|title=Spotlight on Diversity|date=2012-08-31|work=Science {{!}} AAAS|access-date=2018-11-06|language=en}}</ref> Baccouche earned her master's degree from [[Hampton University]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/199904/massmedia.cfm|title=Mass Media Fellows Reflect on Internship Experience|language=en|access-date=2018-11-06}}</ref> in 1998 and her PhD in theoretical nuclear physics from the [[University of Maryland, College Park]], in 2002. <ref>{{Cite news|url=https://vtnews.vt.edu/articles/2011/03/031611-science-baccouche.html|title=Blind physicist Aziza Baccouche to give motivational talk tomorrow|access-date=2018-11-06|language=en}}</ref> Her dissertation entitled "[https://app.box.com/s/kj0tq2r7ud5xwamxj4kpblbzj4qpmh8o Phenomenology of Isoscalar Heavy Baryons]" focused on [[Baryon|heavy baryons]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EHz689TA4OIC&q=Aziza+Baccouche&pg=PA488|title=Baryons 2002: Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on the Structure of Baryons : Jefferson Lab, Newport News, Virginia, USA, March 3-8 2002|last1=Carlson|first1=Carl|last2=Mecking|first2=Bernhard A.|date=2003|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=9789812704887|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www2.phy.ilstu.edu/~johns/documents/PhysicsinYourFutureAPS.pdf|title=Physics in Your Future|website=APS|access-date=2018-11-06}}</ref> She attended a private elementary school in Tunis named Jeanne D’Arc. The school was not equipped to teach visually impaired students.  In the 6th grade a national exam that all elementary students had to pass in order to go on to secondary school would be administered at the end of the school year.  Her school administrators were very concerned about her ability to pass the exam given her visual constraints.  So a decision was made for me to enroll in the only elementary school for the blind in Tunis.  She reluctantly transitioned to Bir El Kasaa. <ref>{{Cite book |last=Baccouche |first=Ella |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Seeking_Vision.html?id=vCL2zQEACAAJ |title=Seeking Vision: A Memoir of a Legally Blind Doctor of Nuclear Physics Who Dared to Envision Possibilities |last2=Baccouche |first2=Zohra |last3=Elyazgi |first3=Zakaria |date=2020-06-19 |publisher=Lulu.com |isbn=978-1-716-84177-4 |language=en}}</ref> A few days before the beginning of her secondary school year, she started at her new school for the blind in Sousse, Tunisia.  This was a boarding school like the one in Bir El Kasaa. There were no opportunities for extracurricular activities at the school. While many students were musically inclined, there were no instruments and no music returning to the United States instruction.  She studied in Sousse for one year before her family returned to the United States.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Baccouche |first=Ella |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Seeking_Vision.html?id=vCL2zQEACAAJ |title=Seeking Vision: A Memoir of a Legally Blind Doctor of Nuclear Physics Who Dared to Envision Possibilities |last2=Baccouche |first2=Zohra |last3=Elyazgi |first3=Zakaria |date=2020-06-19 |publisher=Lulu.com |isbn=978-1-716-84177-4 |language=en}}</ref> 

== Career ==
As part of an [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Mass Media Fellowship in 1998, Baccouche joined [[CNN]] in Atlanta and was appointed the special science correspondent of the Washington Bureau. <ref name="Physics 2018" /> In 2000, she established ''Aziza Productions ,''<ref name="Roberson">{{Cite web |last=Roberson |first=Stephen |title=Aziza Baccouche |url=https://www.nsbp.org/nsbp-news/bhm-physics-profiles/2017-honorees/14-aziza-baccouche |access-date=2018-11-06 |website=www.nsbp.org |language=en-gb}}</ref> a media production company that works with nonprofit organizations to make films that raise awareness about Black or disabled scientists. Baccouche would later preview the show ''Hanging With Dr. Z'' at a festival sponsored by the American Association for the Advancement of Science. <ref>{{Cite web |title=AAAS Video Contest Finalists Teach “Science in a Minute” {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-video-contest-finalists-teach-science-minute |access-date=2026-07-22 |website=American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cheryl |date=2021-06-14 |title=Dr. Zohra Aziza Baccouche, physicist, science filmmaker, and disability advocate, passes away |url=https://werepstem.com/2021/06/14/dr-zohra-aziza-baccouche-physicist-science-filmmaker-and-disability-advocate-passes-away/ |access-date=2022-04-27 |website=We Rep STEM |language=en-CA}}</ref>

After completing her PhD, Baccouche continued her career in [[science communication]]. <ref name=":2" /> In addition to continuing to work at ''Aziza Productions'', she became a science correspondent for ''Evening Exchange with Kojo Nnamdi'' on [[Howard University]] Television. <ref name="Roberson" /> Baccouche was involved with initiatives to increase the number of African-American women studying physics. <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cvent.com/events/2018-national-society-of-black-physicists-conference/event-summary-d23414385ab64685bc59cb54de520954.aspx?lang=en|title=2018 National Society of Black Physicists Conference|website=Cvent|language=en|access-date=2018-11-06}}</ref> She worked as a science media producer and was a frequent contributor to the National Society of Black Physicists ([[National Society of Black Physicists|NSBP]]) conferences. <ref>{{Cite web|title=Aziza Baccouche|url=https://www.nsbp.org/nsbp-news/bhm-physics-profiles/2017-honorees/14-aziza-baccouche|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.nsbp.org}}</ref>  In 2020 Baccouche authored a memoir titled "Seeking Vision," chronicling her life from when she was declared legally blind at the age of eight until her fifth brain surgery. <ref>{{Cite book|last1=Baccouche|first1=Ella|last2=Elyazgi|first2=Zohra|last3=Baccouche|first3=Zakaria|title=Seeking Vision|date=2020|publisher=Lulu Com|isbn=978-1-716-84177-4|location=[S.l.]|oclc=1202444453}}</ref>



Shortly thereafter, she was in hospice for almost a week and lost her ability to speak and move. She developed dementia and died from complications from her brain tumor on June 11, 2021. <ref name=":2" />
== Awards and distinctions ==
Baccouche received a HerStory Award at the Women's Federation for World Peace USA National Assembly in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dr. Aziza Baccouche|url=https://www.wfwp.us/herstory-awardees/aziza-baccouche|access-date=2021-06-20|website=Women's Federation for World Peace USA|date=26 October 2013 |language=en-US}}</ref>
